conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the surgery team doctors. You're here today for your scheduled hernia repair, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's right. The right groin hernia has been bothering me more lately, especially when I walk or lift anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had this for a few months now? Has it gotten larger or more painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely bigger. It bulges out when I stand, and sometimes I feel a pulling or aching sensation. It’s not constant, but it’s hard to ignore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ve reviewed your history — you’re about six months out from your liver transplant, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, almost seven months now. I’ve been doing well overall, but this hernia is new since the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common after major abdominal surgeries. The incision site can weaken over time. We’re planning an open repair today — a Bassini repair — to strengthen the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that different from mesh? I’ve heard about mesh being used.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Mesh is common, but given your transplant and immunosuppression, we’re opting for a tissue-based repair to reduce infection risk. The Bassini technique uses your own tissue to reinforce the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’m on a lot of meds already — don’t want to add complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re being cautious. You’re on sirolimus and other immunosuppressants, so minimizing infection risk is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. And I switched from sirolimus to tacrolimus recently — Prograf, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. The transplant team made that change to better manage your kidney function. We’ll need to monitor your tacrolimus levels closely after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I get that checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant clinic will schedule your trough level — probably in a few days. Make sure to go in the morning before your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my diabetes — should I adjust my insulin today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, keep your long-acting insulin — Lantus — as usual. Hold the fast-acting Humalog today since you’re not eating. We’ll manage your glucose in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been checking it at home, and it’s usually around 120 to 140.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good control. We’ll keep an eye on it. Any other concerns before we prep for surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just — how long will I be here? I was told it might be outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We plan to send you home today, but we’ll keep you for observation if you have pain or need help managing it after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you’re back in your room. The surgery went well — you had a moderate-sized indirect inguinal hernia, and we repaired it using the Bassini technique. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. It’s sore, though — more than I expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely normal. We’re going to manage your pain with tramadol — it’s been helping others in your situation. You can also take acetaminophen as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe with my liver? I mean, after the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, acetaminophen is safe at low doses — up to 2 grams a day, which is about six tablets of 325 mg. We’ll avoid higher doses just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know. And tramadol — any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause drowsiness or nausea in some people. We’ll start low and see how you do. You’ll get one now — let us know if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now, Mr. Thompson? On a scale of 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a 6. Better than earlier, but still uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving tramadol every six hours as needed. Because you’re still having significant discomfort, we’re going to keep you overnight for observation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was hoping to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but it’s safer this way. We want to make sure your pain is under control and you’re able to walk and manage on your own before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well overnight. Pain better today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. Maybe a 3 now. I walked to the bathroom without too much trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. The incision looks clean and dry. You can remove the dressing tomorrow. Showering is okay — just pat it dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No baths or swimming, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly — no soaking for at least a week. Also, no lotions or powders on the incision. And wear sunscreen if you’re outside — your skin is more sensitive with the meds you’re on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds — anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes — you’re now on tacrolimus instead of sirolimus. Take four capsules every 12 hours. Get your levels checked as the transplant clinic directs. Also, we’re adding iron — ferrous sulfate — three times a day for mild anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And Lasix? I wasn’t on that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a low dose — 40 mg daily — to help with any fluid retention. Your kidney function is stable, but we’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have a fever or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the transplant clinic immediately if you have fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or increased abdominal pain. Even small issues can be serious with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to go home when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You’re doing well — ambulating, pain controlled, eating and drinking. You’ll follow up with your surgeon in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set, Mr. Thompson. Here’s your prescription list and instructions. Take tramadol as needed for pain, but not more than every six hours. Acetaminophen up to six tablets a day if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no driving on tramadol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct — avoid driving or heavy machinery until you’re off it. And no lifting more than 10 pounds for four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will come in to go over your meds one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember — the steri-strips will fall off on their own. Don’t pull them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, you’re cleared to go home. Have a safe trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.
